column2: Which claim does buying ordinary shares give an investor in the issuing company?
column3: Ownership of part of the company
column7: An ordinary share represents part ownership. The holder participates in distributions and ordinarily votes without a contractual right to interest.

column2: A profitable company retains all earnings. What is ordinarily due to its ordinary shareholders for that year?
column6: A fixed return on issue price
column7: Earning a profit does not create an automatic dividend. The company can retain its earnings.

column2: On liquidation, where do preference shareholders normally rank relative to unsecured creditors and ordinary shareholders?
column7: Creditors have priority over equity. Preference shares normally carry better distribution rights than ordinary shares in liquidation.

column2: Which feature lets an unpaid preference dividend carry forward to a later year?
column7: Cumulative preference shares preserve arrears. Participation concerns the possibility of sharing in additional distributions.

column2: An issuer needs new funds and invites subscriptions solely from institutions selected by its bookrunner. Which method fits?
column7: A placing targets selected investors. Open offers and rights issues invite existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings.

column2: A founder sells an existing block to the public without issuing new shares. Who receives the proceeds before fees?
column7: An offer for sale disposes of an existing holding. The cash goes to its seller.

column2: A company with widely held shares seeks a Hong Kong listing without marketing or selling securities. Which method fits?
column7: An introduction admits existing, sufficiently widely held securities to trading. It does not require a fund-raising offer.

column2: A holder owns 1,800 shares before a one-for-six rights issue. How many new shares form the entitlement?
column7: Each six existing shares qualify for one new share, so 1,800 divided by six gives 300. The enlarged holding after full take-up would be 2,100.

column2: How may an investor realise value from tradable nil-paid rights without subscribing for new shares?
column3: Sell the entitlement in its dealing period
column4: Claim the issue discount from the registrar
column5: Ask for shares at the subscription price
column6: Wait for the rights to convert at expiry
column7: Nil-paid rights can be traded during their dealing period. Subscribing for the shares themselves requires payment.

column2: What distinguishes an open offer from a tradable rights issue for existing Hong Kong shareholders?
column5: The new shares must be issued at par
column6: Existing investors must take up their shares
column7: Existing shareholders may subscribe under both arrangements. The opportunity to trade the entitlement is absent in an open offer.

column2: Four existing shares trade at HK$15 each. A one-for-four issue offers new shares at HK$10. What is the theoretical ex-rights price?
column7: Four shares worth HK$60 plus HK$10 in new capital give HK$70 across five shares. Market trading can produce a different price.

column2: A one-for-three bonus issue covers all ordinary shareholders equally. What happens to an investor's ownership percentage?
column7: Every eligible holding increases in the same proportion as the total shares outstanding.

column2: How many shares does a holder of 600 own after a two-for-five bonus issue?
column7: The bonus adds 600 times two-fifths, or 240 shares, to the original holding.

column2: A portfolio buys a share on its ex-dividend date. Who keeps the entitlement to the distribution just declared?
column7: Once a share trades ex-dividend, buying it does not confer the payment already detached from it.

column2: A stock trades at HK$36 and has trailing earnings of HK$2.40 per share. What is its trailing P/E?
column7: Divide the share price by the earnings per share. The reciprocal is an earnings yield, rather than a price multiple.

column2: A share earns HK$1.50 this year. What valuation would a comparable multiple of 12 times earnings imply?
column7: Multiplying earnings per share by the assumed comparable P/E gives HK$18. The result depends on the applicability of that multiple.

column2: How does a forward P/E differ from a trailing P/E calculated at the same share price?
column3: Current price divided by estimated earnings
column4: Expected price divided by reported earnings
column5: Current price divided by dividends paid
column6: Forecast dividends divided by current price
column7: The forward multiple relates today's price to estimated future earnings. The trailing multiple uses earnings already reported.

column2: A share priced at HK$24 paid total dividends of HK$1.20 over the last year. What is its historical dividend yield?
column7: Dividend yield is annual dividends per share divided by the current price. HK$1.20 divided by HK$24 is 0.05.

column2: A share starts at HK$40, pays HK$2 and ends at HK$42. What is the simple holding-period return before fees?
column7: The HK$2 gain and HK$2 dividend both belong in the return. Divide the HK$4 total by the HK$40 purchase price.

column2: A constituent starts with an 8% index weight and gains 5%. All others are flat. What is the index return?
column7: Multiply the starting portfolio weight by the price return. With no changes in shares or other constituents, 0.08 times 0.05 is 0.004.

column2: A company has 200 million shares at HK$9 and a free-float factor of 40%. What is its adjusted market value before capping?
column7: Full market capitalisation is HK$1,800 million. Multiplying by 0.40 gives HK$720 million attributable to the eligible float.

column2: How does a Hang Seng gross total return index treat ordinary cash dividends?
column7: The gross version assumes reinvestment before withholding tax. The net total return version uses the after-tax amount.

column2: Two otherwise equal index constituents have different capping factors. Which carries more weight?
column3: The one with the higher factor
column4: The one with the lower factor
column6: Their weights depend on the index divisor
column7: The index formula multiplies the free-float-adjusted value by the capping factor. A smaller factor scales a constituent's contribution down.

column2: A company incorporated in mainland China lists equity in Hong Kong. Which designation applies to its Hong Kong shares?
column7: H shares are issued by mainland-incorporated companies and listed in Hong Kong. The place of incorporation distinguishes them from red chips.

column2: A mainland state entity controls a Hong Kong-listed company incorporated in Bermuda. Which conventional classification fits?
column7: Red chips are incorporated outside mainland China and controlled by mainland entities. A listing venue alone cannot determine the category.

column2: Which transaction illustrates partial privatisation of a government-owned company?
column3: Selling part of the state's stake to investors
column4: Issuing the company's first retail bond
column6: Replacing a subsidy with a bank loan
column7: Partial privatisation transfers part of the ownership to private investors. Hong Kong used a public share sale for part of its MTR holding.

column2: An investor applies for IPO shares. Where should she check when the allocation results will be announced?
column7: The prospectus specifies the announcement arrangements. It also describes how subscriptions will be handled.

column2: A board lot is 500 shares. How does HKEX classify a separate sale of 180 shares?
column7: The quantity is smaller than one board lot. A transaction larger than one lot but not a whole number of lots can instead be a special lot.

column2: Two equal-priced buy orders rest on the Hong Kong continuous order book. Which normally receives an execution first?
column7: Continuous matching gives time priority at the same price. Size alone does not move a later order to the front.

column2: What happens to the unfilled balance of a Hong Kong special limit order after matching?
column6: It carries to the next day
column7: A special limit order can execute at eligible prices but does not leave a resting balance. An enhanced limit order can leave a balance at its input price.

column2: Which Hong Kong auction order specifies a maximum purchase price?
column7: The at-auction limit order specifies a price constraint. An unpriced at-auction order seeks execution at the final equilibrium price.

column2: A share trades on Tuesday under Hong Kong's normal T+2 cycle. With no holidays, which day is settlement due?
column7: Tuesday is the trade date. Counting two settlement days gives Thursday.

column2: What is the legal position of an investor who buys a company's conventional bond?
column7: The investor lends to the issuer and is entitled to the contractual payments. Ownership of the company's equity is a different claim.

column2: A note resets its coupon each quarter to a benchmark plus a fixed margin. Which instrument is it?
column7: The reference rate determines the next coupon when the rate resets. The agreed margin can remain constant while the payment changes.

column2: A bondholder can exchange a note for shares in the issuing company on specified terms. Which feature does she hold?
column7: A conversion provision lets the investor take equity under the agreed terms. A call provision gives the issuer an early redemption right.

column2: Which feature distinguishes a mortgage bond from an unsecured corporate bond?
column7: The pledged asset provides security for the debt. Coupons, maturity dates and credit ratings can apply to either kind of bond.

column2: A borrower calls a bond after market rates fall. Which risk materialises for its holder?
column3: Reinvestment of proceeds at a lower yield
column4: Credit loss on an unpaid coupon
column7: The investor receives the call payment earlier than the original maturity and may have to invest the proceeds at a lower yield.

column2: A bond has HK$20,000 face value and a 3% annual coupon, payable in equal half-yearly instalments. What is each payment?
column7: Annual interest is HK$20,000 times 3%, or HK$600. Each of the two equal payments is HK$300.

column2: Which period normally determines accrued interest when an interest-bearing bond changes hands between coupon dates?
column7: Interest accrues from issue or the most recent coupon date to settlement. The next full coupon covers more than the buyer's holding period.

column2: A fixed-rate bond pays HK$45 annually and trades at HK$900. What is its current yield?
column7: Current yield divides the annual cash coupon by the purchase price. It leaves out any gain or loss at redemption.

column2: A non-callable 5% annual coupon bond matures at par in one year. Which price implies a yield below 5%?
column7: Buying above par means recovering less principal than the purchase price. At 104 per 100 face value the total payment is 105, giving a yield of about 0.96%.

column2: Which measure uses the contractual early redemption price and date in its return calculation?
column7: Yield to call assumes the specified call happens. It differs from the yield calculated using the original maturity.

column2: Which cash flow does a conventional zero-coupon bond promise between issue and its single redemption date?
column7: The price reflects the present value of the amount due at redemption. There are no intervening coupons.

column2: A zero pays HK$1,210 in two years. At a 10% annual compound yield, what is its price today?
column7: Discount twice by 1.10. Dividing HK$1,210 by 1.21 gives HK$1,000.

column2: A one-year bond pays HK$108 including principal at maturity. At an 8% annual yield, what is its value?
column7: The final coupon and principal are a single cash flow one year away. Divide HK$108 by 1.08.

column2: A bond pays HK$4 after one year and HK$104 after two. The respective discount factors are 0.95 and 0.90. What is its price?
column7: The two present values are HK$3.80 and HK$93.60. Apply each factor to the cash flow at its own date before adding them.

column2: If required yields rise, what happens to the price of an existing non-callable bond with fixed promised cash flows?
column6: It rises by the next coupon
column7: A higher discount rate reduces the present value of each fixed future payment. The coupon amount itself stays the same.

column2: A quoted annual rate of 8% compounds half-yearly at 4% each period. What is the effective annual rate?
column7: A unit of principal grows by 1.04 twice. Subtracting one from 1.04 squared gives 8.16%.

column2: A saver earns 4% nominal interest while prices rise 6%. What is the approximate real return using subtraction?
column7: Subtract the inflation rate from the nominal rate for this approximation. The account balance rises but its purchasing power falls.

column2: Comparable five-year government and corporate bonds yield 3.10% and 4.35%. What is the corporate spread?
column7: The difference is 1.25 percentage points. Each percentage point contains 100 basis points.

column2: An agency downgrades a bond while its promised cash flows stay the same. What has changed directly?
column3: The agency's view of credit risk
column7: A rating expresses an opinion about creditworthiness. Revising that opinion need not change any contract term.

column2: Which yields should an analyst plot to isolate the maturity dimension of a government yield curve?
column3: Same currency and comparable credit quality
column6: Multiple bond issuers on one date at a single term
column7: The curve compares yields at different terms to maturity. Mixing currencies or credit grades adds other sources of yield differences.

column2: One-year government debt yields 4.8%, five-year 4.1% and ten-year 3.6%. What shape does this describe?
column7: The yield declines as maturity lengthens throughout these observations. An inverted curve need not contain any negative yields.

column2: A two-year yield stays at 3% while a ten-year yield rises from 4% to 4.6%. How has the curve between them changed?
column6: It has shifted up in parallel
column7: The long-minus-short spread rises from one to 1.6 percentage points. A parallel shift would move both yields by the same amount.

column2: Which action is the second leg of a dealer's repo after it sells securities for cash?
column4: Issuing additional debt to the buyer
column7: The dealer agrees at the outset to reacquire securities later. The paired transactions provide financing backed by the securities.

column2: In a repo, collateral worth HK$5 million is credited at 96% of market value. What cash advance does it support?
column7: The advance is HK$5 million multiplied by 0.96. The HK$0.2 million difference is the haircut.

column2: Which route gives a Hong Kong bank short-term liquidity against eligible securities in the CMU?
column7: The CMU supports repo arrangements for intraday or overnight liquidity. Paying or collecting a coupon does not provide secured funding.

column2: Who issues Exchange Fund Bills for the account of the Exchange Fund?
column7: The bills are obligations of the Hong Kong SAR Government for the Exchange Fund's account. The clearing and trading institutions have different roles.

column2: An Exchange Fund Bill bought below face value is held to maturity. Where does its income arise?
column7: Exchange Fund Bills are issued on a discount basis and redeemed at par. The price difference provides the investor's return.

column2: What does a successful competitive bidder pay for Exchange Fund Bills under the HKMA tender terms?
column3: Price reflecting its own bid yield
column4: Lowest price accepted for any bidder
column5: Average price of all bids received
column7: Competitive bills are allocated at the individual successful yield bids. The issue price corresponds to the relevant bid yield.

column2: Which channel can a member of the public use for a competitive Exchange Fund Note tender?
column3: One of the eligible market makers
column7: HKMA's note tender arrangements direct public competitive bids through eligible market makers. The retail non-competitive channel operates through HKSCC.

column2: What price information must a retail investor supply in a non-competitive Exchange Fund Note tender?
column6: Both a price and a yield
column7: The investor accepts the price set under the non-competitive allocation rules. The competing bids determine the pricing.

column2: Which organisation provides Hong Kong's infrastructure for settling Exchange Fund Bills and Notes in book-entry form?
column7: The CMU provides debt securities depository and settlement services. A trade can settle by book entry rather than by exchanging paper certificates.

column2: What risk does delivery versus payment principally address when two dealers settle a bond trade?
column3: Loss of principal on one-sided delivery
column4: Changes in interest rates after settlement
column5: Default by the bond issuer at maturity
column7: The cash and securities transfers are linked. This protects against delivering one side without receiving the other.
